stemMd:
To be hired as a translator at the agency, one must pass the agency's certification examination. Miguel has passed the agency's certification examination. Miguel will therefore be hired as a translator at the agency.

The flawed reasoning in the argument above is most closely paralleled in which one of the following?

options.label: A
options.textMd: The clinic's busiest day of the week is Monday. So most of the patients the clinic sees are seen on a Monday.

options.label: B
options.textMd: If the ferry is cancelled, the coast road is closed. The coast road is not closed. So the ferry was not cancelled.

options.label: C
options.textMd: No one may enter the reading room without a reader's card. Yusuf has a reader's card. So Yusuf may enter the reading room.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Cigarette sales have fallen every year since the tax was introduced. The tax must therefore have caused the fall.

options.label: E
options.textMd: Every essay that won the prize was written by a graduate student. So no essay written by an undergraduate was any good.

explanationMd:
First name the flaw in the original, then find the choice that makes the same mistake.

"To be hired, one must pass the examination" states a **necessary** condition: hired $\rightarrow$ passed. The argument then observes that Miguel passed and concludes that he will be hired, which requires the conditional to run the other way: passed $\rightarrow$ hired. Passing may be one hurdle among several — interviews, references, a vacancy. Mistaking a necessary condition for a sufficient one is the error, and in conditional terms it is the same move as affirming the consequent.

Choice (B) reproduces it exactly. "No one may enter without a reader's card" says: may enter $\rightarrow$ has a card. The card is required, not enough on its own; the reading room may also demand an appointment or be closed on Sundays. From "Yusuf has a card" the argument concludes he may enter, reversing the conditional in precisely the original's way.

Check the others by naming each flaw and seeing that it is a **different** one:

- (A) leaps from a fact about which essays won to an evaluative claim about quality, and slides from 'did not win' to 'was not any good'.
- (C) confuses the day with the highest daily count with a majority of the weekly total — a part-versus-whole numerical error, no conditional in sight.
- (D) infers causation from a temporal correlation.
- (E) is a valid contrapositive and contains no flaw at all, which alone disqualifies it from paralleling a flawed argument.

The habit to carry forward: on parallel-flaw questions, put the flaw into a one-sentence description first — here, "treats a requirement as a guarantee" — and then test each choice against that sentence rather than against the original's wording. Watch particularly for phrasings that hide a necessary condition, such as *must*, *only*, *without*, *requires* and *unless*.

distractorRationale.e: The error here is a leap from winning to worth, plus the assumption that anything that did not win was bad. That is a different mistake from reversing a conditional: nothing in this argument states a requirement, so nothing is being treated as a guarantee. It attracts a reader who matches the surface pattern of a universal claim about a group.
distractorRationale.a: This confuses the largest single day's share with a majority of the whole week, a quantitative part-versus-whole error. Monday can be the busiest of six open days while accounting for only a fifth of patients. No necessary condition appears anywhere in the argument, so the flaw cannot be the one in the original.
distractorRationale.d: This infers a cause from the fact that one thing followed another, ignoring alternative explanations such as falling incomes or a separate advertising ban. The original contains no causal claim at all; it is a purely conditional error. Choosing this matches 'the argument is obviously flawed' rather than matching the specific flaw.
distractorRationale.b: This is a valid contrapositive: from 'cancelled implies road closed' and 'road not closed' it follows that the ferry was not cancelled. Since a parallel-flaw answer must reproduce a flaw, an argument with no flaw cannot be correct. It is tempting because it is the choice whose vocabulary of conditions most resembles the original's.

accessibilityText: A short flawed argument: passing a certification examination is required to be hired as a translator; Miguel has passed it; therefore he will be hired. The question asks which answer choice's flawed reasoning is most closely parallel. Five answer choices, labelled A through E, each a short argument. The explanation uses an arrow meaning 'if ... then'; no computation is involved.

Distractors carry four other flaws (evaluative leap, part-versus-whole, correlation-to-causation) plus one valid argument. Tagged to lr-reasoning-patterns per the exam config. independentSolve.workingNotes: The stimulus treats a necessary condition (passing the exam is required to be hired) as sufficient. (c) does the same: a reader's card is necessary to enter ("No one may enter... without"), and the argument concludes Yusuf may enter because he has one. (b) is a valid contrapositive, (d) is a causal flaw, (a) and (e) are different errors.

review.notes: Author abstracted every choice to conditional form first. Two earlier drafts of distractors ('only members may borrow, Dana is a member, so Dana may borrow' and 'every grant goes to a registered charity, the shelter is registered, so it will get a grant') reproduced the original flaw and were discarded; they are recorded here because this item type makes that duplication very easy. Awaiting blind independent solve. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
